meta.title: Who really said "At the center of your being you have the answer"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not in the Tao Te Ching, in any chapter, in any translation. The phrase 'at the center of your being' is Witter Bynner's 1944 English for chapter 47; the sentence around it has no Chinese original and no known author.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'At the center of your being you have the answer'?
meta.ogDescription: No Chinese text exists for it. The one genuine fragment is Witter Bynner's 1944 phrasing of chapter 47 — and Bynner called his book an American version, not a translation.

answer.label: Not Lao Tzu — a modern composite around a 1944 translator's phrase
answer.authorDates: Modern, anonymous · shares a phrase with Witter Bynner’s 1944 English
answer.sourceLine: It is not in the Tao Te Ching. Not in chapter 47, not in chapter 33, not anywhere — and crucially there is no Chinese for it, which for a text this heavily edited and this heavily concordanced is decisive. What is real is one phrase: ‘at the center of your being’ comes from Witter Bynner’s 1944 rendering of chapter 47, a book he pointedly subtitled An American Version. The rest of the sentence — the answer, knowing who you are, knowing what you want — corresponds to nothing in the Chinese, and the one specialist account finds it in no Bynner text either.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: 不出戶知天下；不闚牖見天道。其出彌遠，其知彌少。
trail: We checked the two chapters anyone could plausibly mean, in Chinese and in James Legge’s public-domain 1891 English. Chapter 47: ‘Without going outside his door, one understands (all that takes place) under the sky; without looking out from his window, one sees the Dao of Heaven. The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows.’ Close in spirit — and containing no answer, no self, no wanting Chinese and Legge ↗.

Chapter 33, the other candidate, reads 知人者智，自知者明 — Legge: ‘He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent.’ That is self-knowledge as clarity of sight. It is not ‘the answer is inside you,’ and it is certainly not ‘you know what you want.’

Then we found where the English actually comes from. Witter Bynner, The Way of Life According to Laotzu: An American Version (1944), renders chapter 47 as verse: ‘There is no need to run outside / For better seeing, / Nor to peer from a window. Rather abide / At the center of your being…’ The famous phrase is his.

The quote circulates as part of a longer free-verse poem beginning ‘Always we hope someone else has the answer.’ The best available account — Stefan Stenudd’s catalogue of fake Lao Tzu quotes — reproduces the full poem and cites it to M. J. Ryan’s anthology A Grateful Heart (1994), pp. 248–249, noting that its opening part appears in no Witter Bynner version and in no other Tao Te Ching. We have not inspected a physical copy, so we report it as his finding rather than our own Stenudd’s entry ↗.
source.excerptNote: The opening of chapter 47 in Chinese — the nearest thing in the book to the sentiment, and a useful measure of the distance. In plain English, it says: without going out of his door, one knows all under heaven; the farther he goes, the less he knows. It is about not needing to travel for knowledge. It says nothing about having an answer, or about knowing what you want.

source.rightsNote: There is no ancient original behind the sentence people paste: every word of it is modern — Witter Bynner’s 1944 phrasing plus lines first seen in a 1994 anthology — so nothing on this page is cleared for reuse. What is genuinely old is free: the Chinese is ancient and James Legge’s 1891 English is long out of copyright, so quote either of those. The circulating poem is not safe: Witter Bynner’s 1944 version is not public domain — he died in 1968 — and the added opening lines, whoever wrote them, belong to somebody. Quote Legge if you want a free text. This is not legal advice.
source.useLine: Reuse status uncertain — the phrase is Witter Bynner’s 1944 English (in copyright) and the full sentence first appears in a 1994 anthology. Quote Legge’s 1891 chapter 47 if you need a free text.

author.name: Lao Tzu
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Lao Tzu
author.metaLine: trad. 6th century BC · legendary Chinese sage, reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
author.bio: Lao Tzu is a semi-legendary figure traditionally placed in the sixth century BC and credited with the Tao Te Ching, a book of about five thousand Chinese characters. Two features make him the internet’s favourite false author. The book is short, so anything gnomic can be claimed to be in it without anyone checking — and it has been translated into English well over a hundred times, so wildly different wordings all circulate as ‘Lao Tzu,’ which trains readers to accept any English at all. That is the gap this quote lives in.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one is worth walking through slowly, because it is not a straight invention. It is a real translator’s poetry with new lines grafted on, and the join is invisible unless you know where to look.

items.why: The decisive test for a classical Chinese quotation is whether Chinese exists for it. Here none does. The Tao Te Ching is eighty-one short chapters, fully searchable in the original; nothing in it corresponds to ‘you have the answer’ or ‘you know what you want’ search it yourself ↗.

‘Rather abide / At the center of your being’ is Bynner’s line for chapter 47. He called the book An American Version precisely because he was not claiming a literal translation. The evocative phrase readers respond to is a twentieth-century American poet’s, not a Chinese sage’s.

‘You have the answer; you know who you are and you know what you want’ matches no chapter and no translation. It reads like therapeutic reassurance because that is almost certainly what it is — the leading candidate is an anthology’s framing lines around Bynner’s text, but we could not verify the page.

‘He who knows himself is intelligent’ (Legge) praises self-knowledge as a kind of eyesight. The modern quote asserts something stronger and much more flattering: that the answer is already in you and you need only consult it. Taoism’s actual advice runs the other way — empty yourself, do less, want less.

Quote Investigator has no article on it and Wikiquote’s Laozi page does not list it, in the Misattributed section or anywhere else. It circulates almost entirely through Goodreads, BrainyQuote and coaching blogs, always without a translator’s name — which is the tell.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Lao Tzu, and not a translation of anything. One phrase is Witter Bynner’s 1944 English for chapter 47; the sentence around it has no Chinese source and no known author the investigation ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It tells you that you already have what you need, and it tells you in a calm voice with an ancient signature. That is an extremely effective combination, and it is why the line turns up in coaching decks and graduation speeches rather than in books about Chinese philosophy.

The awkward part is that the actual Tao Te Ching is not very interested in you knowing what you want. Its recurring counsel is to reduce — fewer desires, less contriving, less running about. A saying that congratulates you on your inner clarity has been fitted with the name of a book whose main advice is to stop insisting.
detailsBody: Chapter 47, Legge: ‘Without going outside his door, one understands (all that takes place) under the sky; without looking out from his window, one sees the Dao of Heaven.’
Chapter 47, continued: ‘The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows.’ The subject is knowledge, and the warning is against seeking it by travelling.
Chapter 33, Legge: ‘He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty.’
Both are about clarity and restraint. Neither promises an answer, and neither mentions wanting — except to say, in chapter 33, that being content with your lot is what wealth means.
Legge’s 1891 English is public domain, so you can quote either chapter freely. Bynner’s 1944 lines are not.
context.pull: The phrase everyone loves is a 1944 American poet's. The Chinese has no such sentence.
